newsitem.title: SPAIN: ETA takes deadly revenge for jailed Basque leaders.
newsitem.headline: ETA takes deadly revenge for jailed Basque leaders.

text.p: Basque ETA separatists struck twice in Spain on Monday, killing a Supreme Court judge and an airbase worker in attacks aimed at taking deadly revenge for the recent jailing of leaders of ETA's political wing, officials said.
The judge was gunned down just outside his Madrid home hours after a powerful car bomb exploded in the southern city of Granada, killing a civilian airbase worker and wounding seven.
"This is the voice of ETA, the only way ETA knows how to respond: death and terror," Deputy Prime Minister Francisco Alvarez-Cascos said in a statement.
Earlier, Interior Minister Jaime Mayor Oreja cut short a visit to Israel because of the bombing and said it proved that the time was not ripe for government peace talks with the rebels.
"It's very difficult at times like these to even mention the word negotiation," he told state radio.

ETA (Basque Homeland and Freedom), which has killed some 800 people in its 29-year drive for independence, was relatively quiet last year, making officials cautiously optimistic about finding a negotiated solution in the troubled northern region.
But the attacks on Monday dampened those hopes for peace.

Conservative Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar, who held a previously arranged meeting with the nationalist Basque region president on Monday, said negotiation was not possible while ETA continued to plant bombs and hold two kidnap victims.

According to officials close to the meeting, Aznar said the best arena for developing policy that would advance peace in the region was a pact signed by all non-violent Basque parties in Ajuria Enea nine years ago.
The so-called Ajuria Enea pact aims for peace, but does not set out any conditions for contact among Basques of various factions, thus removing any political fallout from ETA attacks.

The murders on Monday follow a turbulent weekend in the Basque region, where thousands took to the streets to protest at the death of an alleged ETA prisoner, who was found hanged in his cell with his feet and hands tied.

An autopsy report said the prisoner had been depressed for several weeks and had killed himself, but the protesters argued it was murder and chanted slogans: "The people will not forgive" and "Assassins, you have killed another prisoner."
Dozens of people were injured and property was smashed and burned in the ensuing violence.

ETA's political wing Herri Batasuna (HB) has warned that tension was growing in the region, particularly after the Supreme Court summonsed the entire 25-member HB leadership to answer charges that they promoted violence.

Five members have been sent to prison after refusing to appear in court, two have gone to Belgium to promote their cause and one was found hanged in his family home on Monday in what officials said was a suicide.
"We are trying to deal with the repression and political persecution that HB has been suffering in recent days," an HB spokesman told Reuters on Monday.
"We blame the central government for the atmosphere that is developing as a result of their repressive activities," another HB leader told journalists.
The radical Basque politicians, who do not rule out violence as a means to achieve independence, have called on Basques to hold protests and strikes against the jailings.

Last week, HB leader Jon Idigoras issued a veiled warning that the Supreme Court prosecution of the party leaders could lead to further ETA attacks. "It could bring costs to society," he told a news conference. "The actual consequences will not be desired."
Police had stepped up security at courts and judges' homes after finding an ETA hit list in a raid on a Madrid flat believed to have been used by the separatists.
Martinez's name was not on the list and he had not been given any special protection. The judge's death was the fourth ETA assassination this year.
